specPoints.text: describe the past evolution of the universe and the main arguments in favour of the Big Bang theory
describe evidence that supports the Big Bang theory (red-shift and cosmic microwave background - CMB - radiation)

primer.text: Around 14 billion years ago the universe burst from a tiny, scorching, dense point and has been expanding ever since — galaxies race apart, the fastest at the greatest distances. Two observations anchor the theory: galactic red-shift, and the cosmic microwave background, the cooled echo of the early universe's heat.

lessons.title: The Big Bang and the expanding universe
lessons.opening: The universe began about 14 billion years ago from a very small, extremely hot and dense region, then exploded — the Big Bang — and has expanded and cooled ever since. Every point moves away from the others, like dots on an inflating balloon, so galaxy density falls as space itself stretches.
keyPoints: The universe began around 14 billion years ago from a very small, extremely hot and dense region.
The giant explosion that started the expansion is the Big Bang.
The universe keeps expanding and cooling from that initial explosion.
Each point moves away from the others; more distant galaxies recede faster.
Like dots on an inflating balloon, the space between galaxies itself stretches.

low.restatement: Tiny, hot, dense start → explosion → 14 billion years of cooling, stretching space.
low.analogy: Raisin bread rising: the dough (space) swells and every raisin (galaxy) drifts from the others.
low.examPointer: Quote 14 billion years and the hot-dense-small start in the same breath.

medium.restatement: Expansion is metric: separations grow everywhere at once, so recession speed scales with distance and density falls.
medium.analogy: A spreadsheet zoom: magnify the sheet and every cell's gap widens — no cell is 'the middle'.
medium.examPointer: Say 'space itself expands' — galaxies are carried, not fired like bullets.

check.stem: According to the Big Bang theory, the universe began…

options.text: about 14 billion years ago from a very small, hot, dense region
options.explanation: Hot, dense and tiny — then it exploded outward.
A thousand times too recent.

options.text: from a large, cold, empty cloud
options.explanation: The start was small, hot and dense.

options.text: at a fixed moment with no beginning at all
options.explanation: The theory is built on a beginning.

options.text: move away from each other, the distant ones faster
options.explanation: Every point recedes from every other; distance speeds the retreat.
That is contraction, the opposite.

options.text: stay fixed while only light moves
options.explanation: The recession of galaxies is the core observation.
There is no centre to orbit in the expansion.

options.text: the space between galaxies stretches, moving the dots apart
options.explanation: The rubber is space itself, not the galaxies travelling through it.

options.text: galaxies are glued to a fixed sky
options.explanation: The dots move as the balloon inflates.
The dots stay the same size; spacing grows.
The analogy is about stretching space, not debris.

check.stem: As the universe expands, the density of galaxies…

options.text: falls, because the same galaxies occupy more space
options.explanation: Fixed count, growing volume — density drops.
The density of galaxies falls.
Spacing grows, so density cannot hold still.
There are no edges in this model.

check.stem: Tracing the expansion backwards in time leads to…

options.text: galaxies crowding closer until everything was a single point
options.explanation: Run the film backwards and the universe contracts to a point.
Backwards means closer together.
The past is denser, not steady.

options.text: the galaxies merging into the Sun
options.explanation: No single-body merger is implied.

check.stem: Describe the start of the universe according to the Big Bang theory.
check.modelAnswer: Roughly 14 billion years have passed since the universe burst outward from a tiny region that was extremely hot and dense.

check.stem: State what happens to the distances between galaxies as the universe expands.
check.modelAnswer: The distances grow: each point moves away from the others as space stretches.

check.stem: Explain why more distant galaxies recede faster in an expanding universe.
check.modelAnswer: Expansion stretches the space between every pair of points, so the more space lies between two galaxies, the faster the gap grows — distant galaxies recede faster, just as far-apart balloon dots separate quickest.

check.stem: Galaxy A sits twice as far from us as galaxy B. In the same expansion period, compare how far each galaxy's distance from us grows.
check.modelAnswer: Galaxy A's distance grows by about twice as much as galaxy B's, because the stretch of space is proportional to the separation.

lessons.title: Evidence: red-shift and the CMB
lessons.opening: Two observations back the Big Bang. Galactic red-shift shows distant galaxies receding — exactly what an explosion of densely packed matter predicts. And the cosmic microwave background, microwave radiation at about 2.73 K arriving from all directions, is the stretched remnant of the early universe's own hot glow.
keyPoints: Galactic red-shift shows distant galaxies receding, as expected after an explosion.
Light from distant galaxies is red-shifted, evidence that the universe is expanding.
The CMB is microwave radiation, wavelength around 1 mm, from every direction at about 2.73 K.
The CMB is the red-shifted remnant of the early universe's high-energy thermal radiation.
The CMB's uniform profile matches a hot body that has cooled for a very long time.

low.restatement: Red-shift = galaxies receding; CMB = the universe's cooled baby-photo in microwaves.
low.analogy: An echo in a cathedral: the original shout (hot gamma-era glow) is long gone, but the stretched, faded echo fills every corner.
low.examPointer: Both evidence names must appear together in 'describe the evidence' answers — red-shift AND CMB.

medium.restatement: CMB numbers to hold: ~1 mm wavelength, 2.73 K, all-sky uniformity, found in 1964 once telescopes cleared the atmosphere.
medium.analogy: Fading graffiti on a stretching wall: what began as sharp bright paint is now a faint red wash spread across the whole surface.
medium.examPointer: Link the microwave wavelength to red-shifted early-universe radiation — the causal chain is the mark.

check.stem: Which two pieces of evidence support the Big Bang theory?

options.text: galactic red-shift and cosmic microwave background radiation
options.explanation: The two named pillars of the evidence case.
Neither is the cited evidence.
Not cosmological evidence at this level.
Local features, not universe-scale evidence.

check.stem: The cosmic microwave background arrives from…

options.text: all directions, at a generally uniform temperature
options.explanation: Uniformity is the striking property.

options.text: one bright patch of sky only
options.explanation: It comes from everywhere.
The Sun's glow masks it, but is not its source.
It is cosmic, not terrestrial.

check.stem: Why is the early universe's radiation now microwave?

options.text: the expansion stretched its wavelength over about 14 billion years
options.explanation: High-energy gamma-era light lengthened into microwaves.
It started far higher in energy.
Stretching, not absorption, did it.

options.text: the radiation cooled by colliding with dust
options.explanation: The wavelength grew with the expansion.
The measured background temperature.
A hundred times too warm — that is 0 °C.
Millions of times too warm.
The background is slightly above absolute zero.

check.stem: Why did the microwave evidence stay hidden until telescopes reached orbit?

options.text: the atmosphere absorbs microwaves, and space flight later lifted telescopes above it
options.explanation: Atmospheric absorption hid the background until orbiting telescopes flew.
Telescopes existed for centuries.

options.text: the CMB had not yet reached Earth
options.explanation: It fills the sky constantly.

options.text: no one had thought of the Big Bang
options.explanation: The theory preceded the discovery.

check.stem: Name the two main pieces of evidence for the Big Bang.
check.modelAnswer: Two pillars: the red-shift of galaxies and the cosmic microwave background — the CMB.

check.stem: State the wavelength region and approximate value of the CMB.
check.modelAnswer: Microwaves, with a wavelength of around 1 mm.

check.stem: Explain why the CMB supports the Big Bang theory.
check.modelAnswer: The early universe was extremely hot and dense, so it must have emitted thermal radiation; the expansion red-shifted that glow over 14 billion years into microwaves arriving uniformly from all directions — a profile exactly like a hot body that has cooled, which rival theories cannot explain.

check.stem: A map of the CMB shows warm patches and cool patches differing by about 0.00001 K. State what the warm patches indicate.
check.modelAnswer: The warmer regions mark a higher density of galaxies, stars and planets.

glossary.definition: The explosion about 14 billion years ago from which the universe expanded.
Microwave radiation, around 1 mm wavelength and 2.73 K, arriving uniformly from all directions — the cooled remnant of the early universe.
The stretching of light from receding galaxies, evidence the universe is expanding.
